text: Howard D. Schultz, born July 19, 1953, to Ashkenazi Jewish parents Fred and Elaine Schultz in Brooklyn, New York, grew up in the Canarsie public housing projects and attended Canarsie High School, graduating in 1971. He studied communications at Northern Michigan University from 1971 to 1975, where he was a member of the Tau Kappa Epsilon fraternity and played football before an injury ended his athletic aspirations. In 1976, he became a salesman for Xerox in New York and in 1979 was recruited by PAI Partners to manage Hammarplast’s U.S. operations, where he visited Starbucks in Seattle in 1981 to fulfill coffee orders. In 1982, at age 29, Schultz joined Starbucks as director of retail operations and marketing. After a trip to Milan, Italy, in 1983, he advocated for introducing espresso beverages, but the original owners, Jerry Baldwin and Gordon Bowker, declined due to concerns about cost, maintenance, and American familiarity with espresso. He left Starbucks in 1985 to open Il Giornale, a specialty coffeeshop, which required $400,000 in funding; Starbucks invested $150,000, local doctor Ron Margolis contributed $100,000, and of 242 investors, 217 rejected the idea. By 1986, he had raised sufficient funds to open Il Giornale, which offered ice cream, minimal seating, and opera music. Two years later, the original Starbucks management sold its retail unit to Schultz and Il Giornale for $3.8 million. Schultz rebranded Il Giornale as a Starbucks store and expanded it across the U.S., emphasizing a social hub model that helped introduce the second wave of coffee culture, especially in Seattle. On June 26, 1992, Starbucks had its initial public offering (IPO), raising $271 million, which financed the doubling of store count. Schultz stepped down as CEO in 2000, succeeded by Orin Smith, and later served as chief global strategist. From 1986 to 2000, and again from 2008 to 2017, he was CEO or interim CEO, with a total of 37 years in leadership roles. During the 2008 financial crisis, he returned as CEO after Jim Donald, leading a mass firing of executives and employees, shuttering hundreds of stores, and temporarily closing all U.S. locations to retrain staff in espresso preparation. He enforced fair trade standards, doubling annual fair trade coffee purchases to 40 million pounds, and appointed the company’s first chief technology officer. He also launched the Starbucks College Achievement Plan in 2014, allowing employees working 20 or more hours a week to access free tuition through Arizona State University. Schultz earned $9.7 million in total compensation in 2009, including a $1.2 million base salary and $7.8 million in stock options. He was an early stakeholder in Jamba Juice (2011) and served on the board of Square, Inc., until 2014. From 2008 to 2017, he oversaw nearly $100 billion in added market capitalization. In 2016, he stepped down as CEO and became executive chairman. On June 4, 2018, he announced retirement from active management, citing a potential presidential campaign. Kevin Johnson succeeded him as CEO, with Myron Ullman as chairman in June 2018. In March 2022, following Johnson’s retirement, Schultz returned as interim CEO until April 2023, when Laxman Narasimhan took over. On March 20, 2023, two weeks before turning over leadership, Schultz stepped down as interim CEO. He appeared before the U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions on March 29, 2023. In January 2001, Schultz led a group of ten investors who bought the Seattle SuperSonics and Seattle Storm from the Ackerley Group for $200 million. He was criticized for running the franchise as a business, particularly in his feud with player Gary Payton over training camp attendance in 2002. In February 2006, he stated the team needed $200 million for arena renovation or a new facility, threatening to sell or move the team if the Washington State Legislature did not approve funding. On July 18, 2006, he sold the SuperSonics and Storm to Clay Bennett for $350 million, after failing to secure public funding for a new arena. Bennett agreed to a one-year "good-faith best effort" to keep the teams in Seattle, a commitment widely disputed. Schultz filed a lawsuit in April 2008 to rescind the sale, claiming fraud and intentional misrepresentation, but dropped it in August 2008. On July 2, 2008, Seattle reached a settlement with the new ownership group, and the SuperSonics moved to Oklahoma City as the Thunder for the 2008–09 season. The sale damaged Schultz’s popularity in Seattle, with a local poll naming him "most responsible" for the team’s departure. In 2019, he accepted full responsibility, calling it one of the biggest regrets of his life. Schultz has written four books: Pour Your Heart Into It (1997, co-written with Dori Jones Yang), Onward (2011, co-written with Joanne Gordon), For Love of Country (2014, co-written with Rajiv Chandrasekaran), and From the Ground Up (2019). The first two books are business memoirs, with Onward praised for its personal and suspenseful account and detailed coverage, though criticized for lacking depth on external criticisms. For Love of Country was called "well-written" and "formidable" by The New York Times Book Review and added to its 2014 Winter Reading List. From the Ground Up, published just before the 2020 U.S. presidential election, was seen as a candidate memoir and received mixed reviews, with some calling it "stunningly boring" and an "autobiography of a pretentious oligarch," though it made the Wall Street Journal bestseller list and was a New York Times bestseller for 2019. Schultz is an outspoken neoliberal, centrist, technocratic, and political independent with positions aligned with the Democratic Party platform, supporting free trade, balanced budgets, tax reform, gun control, and same-sex marriage. He hosted a fundraiser for John Edwards in 2008 and donated to Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign twice ($2,300 each) and endorsed Hillary Clinton in 2016. Since 2012, speculation has arisen about his presidential candidacy, though he declined to run in 2012, 2016, or 2020. He has taken anti-union actions at Starbucks since the late 1980s, disbanding unions when they formed due to corporate resistance. In 2009, a bill known as the Employee Free Choice Act was mentioned in the document. Schultz was named the 209th-richest person in the U.S. by Forbes with a net worth of $4.3 billion in October 2020. He founded the Schultz Family Foundation to support military veterans and combat youth unemployment.

Howard Schultz has supported gun control and universal background checks, and has advocated for comprehensive tax reform, opposing increases in marginal tax rates above 37% and the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, while favoring tax cuts for middle-market and small businesses over large corporations. He is a deficit hawk, viewing the national debt as the greatest domestic threat and criticizing the nation's $400 billion annual sovereign interest payments as unsustainable, though he has been criticized by economists for his stance. Schultz has supported same-sex marriage, with Starbucks expressing support for Washington state's Referendum 74 in 2012 and opposing Seattle's $15 minimum wage ordinance, and in 2013, he publicly told shareholders to "sell their shares" and "buy shares in another company" in response to opposition to Starbucks' stance on same-sex marriage. He has supported a pathway to citizenship for children born in the U.S. illegally, called for greater border security, and opposed President Trump's border wall and executive order banning Syrian refugees, instead advocating for fast-tracking employment for recent immigrants and refugees. Schultz has backed the Employee Free Choice Act, which would allow unions to form via a "card check" instead of secret ballot elections, but lobbied against it in 2009 with CEOs of Costco and Whole Foods, and has historically taken anti-union actions at Starbucks, including disbanding unions after their formation and firing employees involved in union organizing, despite a formal complaint from the National Labor Relations Board. In 2022, during a town hall as interim CEO, Schultz claimed Starbucks was under "assault from unionization" and "outside forces," stating the company did not need an intermediary between management and labor, and one employee was fired just one hour after the town hall. In March 2023, Schultz testified before the U.S. Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions, denying accusations of being a "union buster," and stated he would not follow a ruling by administrative law judge Michael Rosas that found Starbucks engaged in "egregious and widespread misconduct" and required reinstatement of fired employees and rights notifications. Schultz has supported climate action, opposing the U.S. withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and advocating for taxing oil and gas and harnessing wind energy, while criticizing the Green New Deal as economically unrealistic. He has promoted bipartisan governance, encouraging employees in Washington to write "come together" on cups in 2012 and stating he would legislate with bipartisan support if elected, including in Supreme Court appointments. Under his leadership, Starbucks became the first U.S. company to offer healthcare to part-time workers, and he is against Medicare for All and has criticized Republican efforts to repeal the ACA. In 2008, Schultz doubled Starbucks' fair trade coffee purchases, with 65% of coffee being fair trade by 2009 and nearly all by 2015, and signed an agreement with Ethiopia to increase farmer pay and committed to certifying all 747 U.K. stores as fair trade. Schultz is a supporter of free markets, describing the treatment of business as "vilification," and during the pandemic advocated for fiscal stimulus to small businesses, criticizing the PPP as temporary and calling for a federal "Marshall Plan" for small business. In 2015, he founded Onward Veterans to assist post-9/11 veterans and co-authored the book For Love of Country with Rajiv Chandrasekaran, which discussed military service and civilian transition. Schultz married Sheri Kersch in 1982 and has two children; his son Jordan is a sports analyst. He is the 209th-richest person in the U.S. with a net worth of $4.3 billion in October 2020, and as of July 2022, his net worth is $3.9 billion. He owns a 77-meter superyacht named PI, built by Feadship for $120 million. From 2005 to 2019, he reportedly voted in 11 of 38 municipal elections, with The Seattle Times describing his voting record as a "pattern of ignoring many local elections," and Washington Governor Jay Inslee criticized his absence in state politics. Schultz has been described as a foreign policy "liberal hawk," favoring international cooperation and a U.S.-centered unipolar world. He was floated as a potential Democratic candidate in 2012 and 2016, and in 2019 explored a presidential run as an independent, considering a centrist platform and reportedly willing to spend $300 to $500 million, though he later ruled out a run in September 2019, citing overlapping ideologies with Joe Biden and stating he would endorse Biden on September 14, 2020. Schultz has been asked about selling his Starbucks stock if elected, and while not committing to a sale, has expressed interest in setting up a blind trust to manage potential conflicts of interest. He established the venture capital firm Maveron in 1998 with Dan Levitan, which manages $1.3 billion in assets as of July 2014.

The office has prompted calls for Howard Schultz to sell all of his stock holdings in Starbucks to address potential conflicts of interest. Although he has not firmly committed to selling his shares upon election, Schultz has expressed interest in establishing a blind trust to hold his shares. However, Foreign Policy noted that even in a blind trust, his interest in the shares could still create a conflict of interest due to the link between the shares' performance and the company's performance. In 1998, Schultz co-founded the venture capital firm Maveron with investment banker Dan Levitan, primarily investing in start-up companies and consumer-focused seed companies such as eBay, Shutterfly, and Zulily. As of July 2014, the firm had $1.3 billion in assets under management. As of July 2022, Schultz's net worth is US$3.9 billion. Schultz is the owner of 'PI', a 77-metre luxury superyacht built by Feadship for $120 million. In 1996, Howard and Sheri Schultz co-founded the Schultz Family Foundation, which supports Onward Youth, promoting employment for young people aged 16 to 24 who are not in school or working, and Onward Veterans, aimed at helping post-9/11 military veterans transition to civilian life. After the October 7th, 2023 attacks on Israel by Hamas, the Schultz Foundation released a press release on October 13th stating that "we join millions around the world who will not remain silent bystanders to evil" and that "More will follow, including support to address the trauma and humanitarian needs that are unfolding." On October 26, 2023, Starbucks released a press release clarifying Schultz and the company's position, stating that Schultz and the company had never sent profits to the Israeli government or army, without discussing the Schultz Foundation. In 1998, Schultz received the 'Israel 50th Anniversary Tribute Award' for "playing a key role in promoting a close alliance between the United States and Israel." In 1999, AIDS Action awarded Schultz the National Leadership Award for his philanthropic and educational efforts in combating AIDS. Schultz was named Fortune magazine's 2011 "Businessperson of the Year" for his contributions to the economy and job market and was listed as the most generous CEO of 2015 by Fortune for Starbucks' healthcare coverage, educational opportunities, and employee stock options. In 2017, Schultz spoke at the Arizona State University commencement ceremony and was awarded an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters degree. In November 2017, the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund presented Schultz with the National Equal Justice Award.
